slides.title: Start with something easy
slides.text: Here is the graph of a function $f$. Find the point on the graph above $x = 2$ and read its height.
slides.hint: Go to 2 on the x-axis, move straight up to the graph, then read the height on the y-axis.

slides.title: Now walk toward it
slides.text: Forget the point at $x = 2$ for a moment. Drag the slider so $x$ gets close to 2 from the left, then from the right. Watch the height $f(x)$.
slides.after: From both sides, the height closes in on 3.

slides.text: As $x$ gets close to 2, what height is the graph heading toward?
slides.hint: Think back to the slider. What number was $f(x)$ closing in on?
slides.explain: The heights close in on 3. That height is the **limit**: $lim[x->2] f(x) = 3$.

slides.text: The point is gone. Drag toward $x = 2$ from both sides anyway. Where is the graph heading?
slides.after: Still closing in on 3, even though the graph never gets there.

slides.text: $f(2)$ is undefined. What is the limit?
slides.hint: The limit asks where the graph is heading, not what happens at $x = 2$ itself.
slides.explain: Still 3. **A limit is where the graph is heading. It does not matter what happens at the point itself.**

slides.title: When the two sides disagree
slides.text: This graph jumps at $x = 2$. Drag toward 2 from the left, then from the right. Do you get the same height?
slides.after: From the left the height closes in on 1. From the right it closes in on 3.

slides.text: Coming from the left ($x -> 2^-$) the graph heads to 1. From the right ($x -> 2^+$) it heads to 3. What is the two-sided limit $lim[x->2] f(x)$?
slides.hint: The two sides disagree. When that happens the limit does not exist. Use the DNE button.
slides.explain: The sides disagree, so the limit does not exist (DNE). The one-sided limits still exist: $lim[x->2^-] f(x) = 1$ and $lim[x->2^+] f(x) = 3$.

questions.explain: The limit says where the graph is heading. $f(3)$ could be 7, another number, or undefined.

questions.text: A function can have a limit at $x = a$ even if $f(a)$ is undefined.
questions.explain: A graph with an open circle still heads toward that height from both sides.

questions.text: If the left-hand and right-hand limits at $x = a$ are different numbers, the two-sided limit does not exist.
questions.explain: The two-sided limit needs both sides to agree.

options: $f(x)$ gets close to $L$ as $x$ gets close to $a$ from both sides
questions.explain: A limit describes the height the outputs approach as the inputs approach $a$.

options: from the left, through values less than 4
from the right, through values greater than 4
questions.explain: The small minus sign means from the left side, where $x$ is less than 4.

questions.text: $lim[x->1^-] f(x) = 2$ and $lim[x->1^+] f(x) = 5$. What is $lim[x->1] f(x)$?
questions.explain: The sides disagree, so the two-sided limit does not exist. We never average them.

questions.text: $lim[x->1^-] f(x) = 4$ and $lim[x->1^+] f(x) = 4$, but $f(1) = 9$. What is $lim[x->1] f(x)$?
questions.explain: Both sides head to 4. The value $f(1) = 9$ does not affect the limit.

questions.text: If $f(5)$ is undefined, then $lim[x->5] f(x)$ does not exist.
